Welcome {name}, to this interactive story for Linguistics 2210.
[center]~ ~ ~[/center]
Today is {current_date}. To get things started we're going to take a step back - to the summer of 1964.

Our story begins with a young man straddling a 10-speed bicycle, his feet flat on the gravel shoulder of a quiet highway. He's dressed in a white t-shirt, jogging shorts, and sneakers appropriate for a long haul. Bookish, thick glasses frame his face.

He's looking at a large

The highway is not particularly busy - but then again, it never is. Being on the Avalon Peninsula means it's as far off the beaten trail as you can get in Canada.

It's a hot day across the island, an unusual meterological event in Newfoundland, so the man on the bicycle is taking a water break, wiping away sweat and looking at a crisp, white notebook. It's spine is yet to be cracked in any serious way.

else.text:
[center][b]The End[/b][/center]

In this short, interactive, creative, non-fiction narrative you, {name}, witnessed a young Harold Paddock enter the town of Carbonear to start his pioneering work in dialectology.
The dialogue with an older man from Carbonear illustrated how some people might respond to linguistic variation, i.e. Harold using the {accent} accent. This stylistic option that is avaiable to some speakers can be perceived differently, sometimes positively or negatively, depending on the social context.

then.text: In playing this game, you guided Harold in identifying himself as a researcher conducting a study on regional dialects of Newfoundland and Labrador English. You invited the man to participate being sure to elicit his informed consent. Ethical standards in linguistics research ensures researchers get consent from participants in a study, so, GOOD work!

You also helped Harold dutifully record his first dialect finding, noting important details about the speaker:

1. an older man in Carbonear uses the DRAGONFLY variant "[i]'orse-stinger[/i]".
The journal is where Harold would have written down the dragonfly variant if he remembered to. Usually this isn't like him.

Ethical standards in linguistics research ensures researchers get consent from participants in a study. Any attempt to coerce or influence someone without their full and informed consent is a violation of these standards. Remember that Harold needs to follow the protocol.

Harold gives the bicycle a gentle push forward and follows up with a few turns of the pedals. This gives the bike enough momentum to sail into the first driveway just inside the town limits. It's home to a rustic, saltbox house. He spots a man working away in his window garden. Harold raises his hand in a polite wave.

[i]"'ow's she gon', by"[/i], the man calls out.

Harold quickly assesses the man's pronunciation. He's a local. Probably born and raised in this same house. Never left.
